Recommend: compress client-side, then upload directly to object storage via presigned URLs, with your app server only ever touching metadata — not the image bytes.

1. Client selects/captures the photo and resizes it before sending — phone photos run 3-12MB; downscaling to ~1600-2000px on the long edge and re-encoding as JPEG/WebP at ~75-85% gets it to a few hundred KB, which matters a lot on mobile data.
2. Client asks your backend for a presigned upload URL scoped to that listing.
3. Client PUTs the compressed file straight to storage (S3/GCS/R2/etc.), bypassing your API — keeps large binaries off your app tier and gives you per-file progress/retry, which matters on flaky mobile connections.
4. On success, client (or a storage event) tells the backend to record the photo against the listing; thumbnail generation happens async.

Two things actually fork this design, worth pinning down before building:
- Native app vs. mobile web — native gets background upload and resumable retry; web (`<input type=file capture>`) is simpler but the upload has to finish before the tab/browser closes.
- What storage/backend you're already on — some (e.g. Cloudinary) do direct upload + resize for you, making the presigned-URL plumbing unnecessary.

Left out at this depth: EXIF orientation handling, reorder/cover-photo UI, max photo count, offline queuing.

Two forks matter here:

**Upload path**: have the client request a presigned URL from your backend, then PUT the file straight to object storage (S3/GCS/R2) rather than proxying the bytes through your app server. Your server only handles metadata (listing ID, filename, content-type) and never touches the binary — keeps it fast under cellular upload conditions and avoids memory pressure from concurrent large uploads.

**Client-side resize before upload**: phone photos routinely land at 3-15MB and 3000-4000px on a side, which is overkill for a listing photo and slow over cellular. Downscale in the browser/app (canvas or an image-manipulation lib) to something like a 1600-2000px longest edge at ~80% JPEG quality before requesting the presigned URL — this is the single biggest lever for perceived upload speed and storage cost. iOS Safari camera captures often come through as HEIC, so either convert client-side or handle that content-type explicitly.

After the PUT completes, use a storage-triggered event (S3 event → Lambda/queue, or GCS Pub/Sub) to generate thumbnail/display-size derivatives asynchronously and mark the listing photo "ready" — don't block the UI on server-side processing.

Depth I'd leave for later: multi-photo reordering/drag-drop UI, retry/resume for flaky connections, and moderation/EXIF-stripping on ingest.

Cache-aside at the data layer: Redis, keyed by product ID, populated on read-miss, invalidated on write, TTL as a backstop. That's the standard fix when a DB round-trip dominates render time.

Two decisions actually fork the design:

**Is the page identical for every visitor** (no per-user pricing, cart state, or personalization)? If yes, put a CDN/edge cache (Fastly, CloudFront) in front of the whole page with a short TTL plus purge-on-publish — that skips the app server entirely and is the bigger win. If anything on the page is per-user, edge caching is out and you cache only the data layer, still rendering per-request.

**Invalidation: event-driven vs TTL-only.** Event-driven (delete the Redis key when the product is edited, via the admin write path or a webhook) stays accurate but means wiring invalidation into every write path. TTL-only (say 60s) is simpler but serves stale price/stock for that window. For product data I'd do event-driven invalidation with a longer TTL as a safety net for any write path you miss.

Left out: cache stampede protection — when a hot key expires, many concurrent requests can all miss and hit the DB at once; that needs a lock or request-coalescing layer if traffic is high enough to matter.

The CDN in `CDN.md` already sits in front of every request and honors whatever `Cache-Control` the app sends — hit rate is 0% only because `middleware/security.js` slaps `no-store` on everything app-wide, a blanket fix from the 2024 audit that was really about `/account`. `routes/products.js` confirms `/p/:slug` is anonymous and identical for all users. So: stop applying that middleware to `/p`, and give the product route a real `Cache-Control: public, max-age=…` — that alone lets the CDN start absorbing the ~600ms `relatedProducts` join and the ~250ms `stockFor` call for repeat requests, with no new infrastructure.

The one real fork is TTL granularity: `productBySlug`/`relatedProducts` only change when the catalog is edited (a few times a day, per the `db.js` comment), so they tolerate a long TTL fine, but `stockFor` reflects live inventory and will go stale under the same TTL. Decide whether to accept that staleness (e.g. cap it at 30–60s, acceptable if stock isn't shown as an exact real-time count) or pull stock out of the cached HTML entirely (client-side fetch or edge-side include) and cache the rest of the page for hours. Left out: invalidation on admin edits — worth a follow-up once the TTL approach is picked.

The 900ms is almost all in `relatedProducts` (~600ms, a four-table join) and `stockFor` (~250ms) in `db.js` — `productBySlug` is only ~40ms. None of it varies by user: `routes/products.js` reads no session and says price/stock/copy are identical for everyone, and the catalogue only changes via the admin tool a few times a day.

The actual blocker isn't missing cache infrastructure — it's `middleware/security.js`. It applies `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private` to every route, including `/p`, because that was the fastest way to close a 2024 audit finding about `/account/orders` leaking through an intermediary cache. `CDN.md` confirms the CDN already sits in front of every request, honors whatever `Cache-Control` the origin sends, and has a 0% hit rate — entirely because of this blanket header. There's no path-rule option; platform engineering explicitly requires cache policy to live in app headers.

So the fix is scoping, not adding a layer: give `/p` its own middleware with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=<N>, stale-while-revalidate=<M>`, and leave `/account` on the existing no-store. That turns the CDN into a real cache for product pages for free, since it's already terminating every request.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **TTL length** — catalogue edits land a few times a day, so minutes (60–300s) is defensible; use `stale-while-revalidate` so expiry doesn't force a synchronous 900ms hit. Immediate propagation on admin edits would need a purge call instead, which is more moving parts than the staleness window justifies here.
- **Whether `stockFor` needs its own treatment** — it's a coarse inventory sum used for page display, not a reservation check, so it's fine under the same TTL as the rest of the page. If checkout ever reads this same function for a real availability decision, that path would need to bypass the cache.

Left out: purge-on-admin-edit, and whether uncached/long-tail slugs still hammer the DB directly (an app-level cache for `relatedProducts` only matters if CDN coverage turns out incomplete, e.g. very large catalogue with a long tail of rarely-hit slugs).

Enforce it at the edge (gateway/reverse proxy or API gateway middleware), not deep in app code — that's what stops the offending client's requests before they consume the same worker/DB resources everyone else needs, which is the actual problem you have.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Key by client identity, not IP.** Rate limit on the API key/auth token. IP-based limiting misses clients behind shared NAT/proxies and can't distinguish "this specific client" from others sharing an address — you need to isolate the one hammering you.
2. **Token bucket over fixed/sliding window.** It absorbs legitimate bursts while still capping sustained rate, and it's cheap to implement with a Redis `INCR`+TTL or Lua script if you're running multiple instances (in-memory counters only work if there's a single instance or you accept per-instance limits that are N× looser than intended).

On limit: return `429` with a `Retry-After` header so well-behaved clients back off instead of retrying blindly.

Left out: what the per-client quota should actually be, tiered limits for different client classes, and the Redis-script details for atomic distributed counting — those are the next layer down once you pick the above.

Key the limiter on `client_id`, not IP — the comment in `routes/api.js` already notes clients share NAT addresses and one client can call from many, so IP-keying would either throttle the wrong tenant or miss the offender.

Enforce it in that same middleware, right after the DB lookup resolves `req.client` — you already pay a round trip there, and Redis (`redis.js`) is the one piece of state shared across all 4 workers per box and across boxes, so it's the natural place to count. Implement it as a token bucket via a small Lua script (atomic read-refill-decrement) keyed by `ratelimit:{client_id}`, rather than a plain `INCR`+`EXPIRE` fixed window — a fixed window lets the noisy client burst right up to the boundary twice in a row, which is the exact "degrading it for everybody else" pattern you're trying to stop. Return `429` with `Retry-After` when the bucket's empty.

Left for the next layer: the Lua script itself, and whether the limit is flat or driven by `req.client.plan`.

Looking at the actual code: `app.js` clusters 4 workers per box with nothing shared in-process, `redis.js` already gives every worker a shared Redis client, and `routes/api.js` resolves `req.client.client_id` from the API key before anything else runs.

Key by `client_id`, not IP — the comment in `routes/api.js` says clients share NAT'd IPs and single clients call from many IPs, so IP-based limiting both over- and under-blocks. Count in Redis, not in-process: since `cluster.js` forks 4 independent processes per box with no shared memory, an in-process counter only ever sees a slice of one client's traffic. Add the check as middleware in `routes/api.js`, right after the key lookup and before the route handlers touch Postgres, so a hammering client gets a 429 before it reaches the db pool that's likely the actual bottleneck degrading everyone else.

Two decisions that fork the implementation:
- **Algorithm**: `INCR`+`EXPIRE` on a `rl:{client_id}:{window}` key is one Redis round trip and enough to stop a noisy neighbor. A token-bucket Lua script is more accurate at window boundaries but is the next level down.
- **Limit source**: `api_keys` already has a `plan` column, so limits can be per-plan instead of one global number.

Left out: response shape (429 + `Retry-After`), and whether the limit is global per client or per-route.

WebSocket/SSE push is ruled out by the platform itself: `PLATFORM.md` says connection upgrades 501 at the edge and instances freeze between invocations, so nothing can hold a connection open or run a background timer to push updates. That leaves polling — and since `jobs/rollup.md` says the data only changes once a minute, on a fixed schedule, the real design decision isn't push vs. poll, it's how the poll is shaped:

- Replace the click handler in `public/dashboard.js` with a loop that polls just after the known minute boundary (e.g. :05), not a naive tight `setInterval`. Polling faster than the data can change just burns serverless invocations for no new data.
- Make idle polls cheap: have `api/metrics.js` compare the client's last-seen `computed_at` (ETag/If-None-Match, or a cheap query) and return 304 instead of re-shipping the same 4KB payload when nothing rolled over yet.
- Pause polling on `visibilitychange` so tabs left open overnight stop invoking the function.

Left out: retry/backoff on a failed poll, and coordinating multiple tabs open to the same dashboard so they don't each poll independently — both real, but secondary to schedule-aligned polling, which is the piece that actually matters given these constraints.

Two forking decisions:

**Push vs. poll.** Polling (client re-fetches every N seconds) is simplest and fine for most ops dashboards where "real-time" really means "within 10-30 seconds." Push (WebSocket or Server-Sent Events) is worth it only if updates need to be sub-second or the polling interval would otherwise hammer your backend with many open dashboards.

**Recommendation:** start with SSE from a single backend endpoint that streams updates — simpler than WebSockets (no bidirectional handshake needed, works over plain HTTP, auto-reconnects in browsers), and avoids the wasted-request problem of polling. The frontend keeps a persistent connection and patches state on each event.

What I'm leaving out: how the backend gets notified of changes to push (DB triggers/CDC vs. an internal pub-sub the write path publishes to) — that's the harder half and depends on where your data currently lives.

Given the platform notes: WebSockets are dead at the edge (501), functions get frozen/killed at 10s with no sticky routing, and `rollup` only changes once a minute via a fixed cron job. That rules out anything socket- or push-based — polling is the only option the platform actually supports, and since the data can't change faster than once a minute, polling is not a compromise here, it's the correct fit.

Build it as: `dashboard.js` replaces the load-once/click-to-refresh pattern with `setInterval(load, ...)` calling the existing `/api/metrics` endpoint (no backend change needed — it's already cheap, 4KB/30ms, `no-store`). Two decisions actually fork the design:

- **Interval + skip-render logic**: poll every 20-30s (a few times per rollup cycle, not exactly 60s, so you don't beat-frequency against the job's on-the-minute schedule) and compare the returned `computed_at` to the last one — only re-render when it changed, so the UI doesn't flicker every poll for nothing.
- **Pause when hidden**: use the `visibilitychange` event to stop polling on background tabs and fetch immediately on refocus, so idle tabs aren't hammering `/api/metrics` all day.

Left out: retry/backoff on a failed fetch and any user-visible "stale/error" indicator — worth adding but a separate decision from the polling mechanism itself.

The core fork: a timeout means you don't know if the charge went through, so you can't just re-fire the same request — you need an idempotency key reused across attempts, and a way to reconcile with the provider before deciding to retry vs. mark success.

Shape I'd build:

1. **Idempotency key per attempt group**, generated once per checkout and sent on every retry of that charge. Store it against the order/invoice row.
2. **On timeout specifically** (not on a decline — declines are definite, don't retry those): don't immediately re-request. Query the provider's charge-status endpoint for that idempotency key first. If it shows succeeded, mark paid and stop. If it shows failed/not-found, retry.
3. **Retry out-of-band**: return the customer a "processing" state, not "payment failed," and do the retry in a background job with backoff (e.g. a few attempts over seconds-to-minutes) rather than blocking the original request further.
4. **Cap attempts**, then surface a real failure state distinct from "processing" — only say "payment failed" once you've confirmed it, not on the first timeout.

The one thing this depends on that I can't verify without seeing your provider integration: whether your gateway supports idempotency keys and a status-lookup call (Stripe, Braintree, Adyen all do). If it doesn't, you'd need a different reconciliation path — worth checking which gateway you're on before locking this in.

The fork here isn't really "retry or not" — it's idempotency. `PROVIDER.md` is explicit: a Cardstream timeout means the charge state is **unknown**, not failed, and the vendor's fix is the `Idempotency-Key` header, which `payments.js` never sends. Retrying without it risks double-charging on exactly the timeouts you're trying to fix.

- Generate one idempotency key per charge attempt and persist it on the `orders` row *before* calling `charge()` (not just in-memory), so a retry — even one triggered by a fresh request after the process died — reuses the same key instead of minting a new one.
- Pass that key as `Idempotency-Key` in `payments.charge()`, and have it (or a thin wrapper) retry on timeout/network error a bounded number of times with backoff, rather than letting `checkout.js` treat the first rejection as final.
- If retries are exhausted, still don't show "payment failed" — since Cardstream won't confirm failure either — move the order to a `payment_unknown`/`pending` state and resolve it out of band (webhook, or a reconciliation job that checks status by idempotency key).

Retry count, backoff schedule, and how reconciliation gets kicked off are the next level down.

Treat a timeout as "unknown," not "failed" — retry against the gateway using the *same idempotency key* as the original attempt, so a charge that actually succeeded slowly doesn't get double-charged. Wrap the charge call in 2–3 retries with capped exponential backoff (e.g. 1s/2s/4s) within the same request, and only show "payment failed" once retries are exhausted *and* a status check confirms no charge exists.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Idempotency key scope**: generate one key per checkout attempt (not per HTTP call) and reuse it across all retries — without this, retrying a timeout is exactly what causes double charges.
- **Sync vs async retry**: at "a few times a day," inline synchronous retry (customer waits a few extra seconds) is simpler and sufficient; go async (return "processing," retry in background, update via webhook) only if timeouts can run longer than a customer will tolerate waiting on the request.

Left out: gateway-specific idempotency-key semantics (varies by provider) and a reconciliation job for the rare case where status is still unresolved after retries.

At 38k rows, Postgres full-text search fits — no case for pulling in Elasticsearch/Algolia at this scale, and it stays in the existing `pg` connection.

Add a generated `tsvector` column weighting `name` above `description`, with a GIN index:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vector tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

Then a route alongside the existing `GET /` in `routes/products.js`, using `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles raw user phrases better than `plainto_tsquery`) and `ts_rank` for ordering, filtered on `active` like the other queries.

Two decisions that actually fork this:
- **Typo tolerance.** Plain FTS won't match "wireles" to "wireless." If that matters, add `pg_trgm` with a trigram GIN index and blend it in (or fall back to it when FTS returns nothing) — worth deferring until you see real query logs show it's needed.
- **Result ranking beyond text relevance.** If "best" match should also weigh popularity/recency rather than pure `ts_rank`, that's a second scoring input, not a text-search problem — decide separately.

Left out: pagination/debouncing on the client side, and multi-word AND-vs-OR query semantics — both straightforward once the above is in place.

Index `name` and `description` into a full-text search structure and rank matches against the typed words, weighting name matches above description matches.

For most catalogs, Postgres full-text search (a `tsvector` column with a GIN index, weighted `name` higher via `setweight`) is the right complexity — it's already in your database and handles a few keywords fine, including basic stemming. Move to a dedicated engine (Meilisearch, Typesense, or Elasticsearch) only if you need typo-tolerance/fuzzy matching or the catalog is large enough that DB-side search gets slow — that's the one fork worth deciding early, since it decides whether search lives in the app DB or a separate service you now have to run and sync.

Direct-to-storage upload with async processing is the standard shape: browser gets a presigned URL from your backend, uploads straight to object storage (S3/GCS/R2), then a background job generates thumbnails and a display-size variant. This avoids routing multi-megabyte phone photos through your app server.

The forks that actually matter for you:

**Where resizing happens.** Phone cameras produce 3-15MB files, often HEIC. Resize/compress client-side before upload (canvas or `createImageBitmap`, cap the long edge around 2000px, re-encode to JPEG/WebP) — cuts upload time and storage cost, and sidesteps HEIC-decoding gaps in browsers that aren't Safari. Still generate a proper thumbnail server-side afterward since you can't trust the client output for anything you'll depend on (consistent aspect ratios, watermarking, etc.).

**Upload path.** Presigned PUT URL from your server, uploaded directly by the client, is simpler and cheaper than proxying bytes through your app. The backend only handles a `POST /listings/:id/photos/init` (returns presigned URL + photo id in "pending" state) and a completion callback or S3 event webhook to flip it to "ready" once the object exists.

**Data model.** A `photos` table keyed by listing, not a single-URL column — sellers attaching multiple photos, needing ordering/cover-photo, and needing to delete one without touching the rest is the common case, and retrofitting that later is painful.

What stack are you on (mobile web, native app, which backend/storage)? That decides the concrete APIs underneath this.

Recommended shape: client resizes/compresses the photo before sending (phone originals run 10-25MB HEIC/JPEG, way more than a listing needs), then uploads directly to object storage via a short-lived presigned URL your API issues — the API never touches the binary, just records the resulting key against the listing once the upload completes. A background job then generates thumbnails and strips EXIF/GPS data from the original.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **Direct-to-storage vs. proxy through your server** — direct is the right default at any scale beyond a toy app, since it keeps large binaries off your API tier.
- **Client-side compression vs. trusting the server pipeline to downsize** — client-side saves upload bandwidth on mobile connections, but means shipping a resize step (e.g. canvas/HEIC-decode) into the app.

Left out: multi-photo ordering/reordering, retry/resume for flaky mobile networks, and moderation/virus-scanning — worth designing once these two forks are settled.

Direct-to-storage upload with presigned URLs: the client requests a short-lived signed URL from your API, uploads the photo straight to object storage (S3/GCS/R2), then reports back the object key to attach to the listing. Phone photos run 3–12MB each; routing that through your app server just to relay it to storage burns server memory and bandwidth for no benefit.

The two decisions that actually fork this:

1. **Where resizing happens.** Phone cameras produce oversized originals (and iOS defaults to HEIC). Resize/re-encode client-side before upload to cut upload time and avoid format issues, or accept the original and normalize server-side via a background job triggered on upload completion (storage event or webhook), producing a display size and a thumbnail. Client-side is faster for the seller; server-side guarantees consistent output regardless of device. Most listing apps do both — client-side downscale for speed, server-side re-encode for a canonical thumbnail.
2. **Multi-photo state before the listing is saved.** Sellers typically add photos before the listing exists as a row, so uploads need to attach to a draft/session, not a listing ID — otherwise you're blocked on create-listing-first, upload-photos-second ordering.

Left out: the actual resize/thumbnail pipeline, retry/resumability for spotty mobile connections, and CDN/serving setup — all a level down from this.

Cache-aside with Redis in front of the DB queries, not a full-page cache: key by product ID (plus locale/currency if those vary the response), TTL of a few minutes as the safety net, and explicit invalidation (delete the key) on product update/price/inventory writes so edits show up immediately rather than waiting out the TTL.

Two decisions actually fork this:
- **What you cache** — raw query results vs. the fully assembled page/API response. Cache the assembled response (post-joins, post-formatting); it saves more work per hit and avoids re-running assembly logic on every request.
- **Stampede handling** — a popular product's key expiring under load can send a burst of requests to the DB at once. Use request coalescing (single in-flight DB fetch per key, others wait on it) or jittered TTLs so expirations don't cluster.

Left out: cache warming/pre-population for known high-traffic products, and whether a CDN layer sits in front of this for fully anonymous/cacheable pages — worth a follow-up if product pages are mostly the same for every visitor.

Cache `/p` at the edge, not in the app. The CDN already sits in front of every request and only caches what origin headers allow — its 0% hit rate is caused entirely by `middleware/security.js`, which forces `no-store` on every route, including `/p`. Product pages are anonymous and identical for every visitor (per the comment in `routes/products.js`), which is exactly what an edge cache is for — a cache hit skips the ~600ms `relatedProducts` join and the ~250ms `stockFor` query entirely.

Two decisions actually fork this:

1. **Don't touch `security.js` globally.** Its blanket `no-store` was the fix for the 2024 finding where an account page leaked across users in an intermediary cache — loosening it app-wide risks reopening that on `/account`. Override `Cache-Control` per-route in `routes/products.js` after the shared middleware runs, e.g. `public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=60`, and leave `/account` alone.
2. **TTL vs. invalidation.** Catalog edits happen only a few times a day, so a short fixed TTL is enough to eliminate the DB hit on nearly all traffic with zero new infrastructure. Only build push-based CDN purge from the admin save handler if a few minutes of staleness after an edit is unacceptable.

Left for the next level: whether `stockFor` belongs in the cached response at all, since inventory can move faster than catalog content — that's a call about how fresh stock needs to be on this page, not a caching-mechanism question.

Cache-aside in front of the DB: Redis, keyed by product ID, storing the assembled product data (or the slow query's result), with a TTL plus explicit invalidation fired on product update/price change. That turns the 900ms into a sub-10ms hit without touching rendering logic, and product data changes rarely enough that staleness risk is low.

The fork that decides the bigger design: is the page identical for every visitor, or does it bake in per-user pricing/cart/inventory? If identical, skip the data cache and full-page-cache at the CDN/edge instead (bigger win — kills the request before it reaches your servers), invalidated by a purge webhook on update. If it's personalized, fragment out the personalized bits and cache the rest, or fall back to the data-layer cache above.

Key insight from the code: `routes/api.js` already resolves `req.client.client_id` (and `plan`) from the API key before anything else runs, and Redis (`redis.js`) is the one thing shared across the 4 cluster workers per box and across boxes — so that's exactly where a rate limiter's counters need to live, since in-process state (a `Map`, a counter variable) wouldn't be shared between workers or boxes.

Recommendation: a token-bucket counter in Redis, keyed by `client_id` (not IP — the auth comment notes clients share NAT'd addresses, so IP-keying would punish innocent neighbors and under-punish the offender), implemented as a small Lua script (`EVAL`) so the check-and-decrement is atomic despite many workers hitting Redis concurrently. Add it as another `router.use` in `routes/api.js`, right after the auth middleware — it already has `req.client.plan` loaded, so the bucket size/refill rate can vary by plan for free. Return `429` with `Retry-After` on rejection.

The one real fork: token bucket (Lua script, atomic, allows short bursts, no boundary thundering-herd) vs. plain `INCR`+`EXPIRE` fixed window (fewer moving parts, but two `Redis` round-trips aren't atomic together and traffic can double up at window edges). Token bucket is worth the extra script given this is a shared-fate resource across all boxes.

Rate limit by `req.client.client_id` (set by the existing auth middleware in `routes/api.js`), not by IP — the comment there already notes multiple clients share a NAT'd address, so IP would punish innocent clients and let a key-rotating abuser slide through.

Enforce it centrally in the `redis.js` instance, since the four cluster workers share nothing else in process memory and requests for the same client can land on any worker or any box. A per-worker in-memory counter would only catch 1/4 of that client's traffic per box. Add a middleware right after the key-lookup one that runs an atomic Redis Lua script (INCR/EXPIRE or a token-bucket script) keyed on `ratelimit:{client_id}`, checks it against a limit chosen from `req.client.plan`, and returns 429 with `Retry-After` when it trips.

Left for the next level down: token-bucket vs. fixed/sliding-window counter semantics, and the actual Lua script for atomicity.

Key constraint from `app.js:9-11`: 4 cluster workers per box, "nothing in module scope is shared" — any in-process counter (like `express-rate-limit`'s default memory store) undercounts by ~4x per box and doesn't see other boxes at all. The only cross-process state you have is Redis (`redis.js`), already used for sessions, so counters have to live there too.

Key the limiter on `client_id`, not IP — `api.js:6-8` calls out that clients share NAT addresses, so IP-based limiting would throttle innocent clients sharing a NAT with the abusive one. The auth middleware in `api.js:9-19` already resolves `req.client.client_id` from the API key before any route runs, so add the limiter as a second `router.use()` right after it, before `/reports` handlers — it gets the key for free and unauthenticated requests never reach it.

For the counter itself, a fixed-window `INCR` + `EXPIRE` in Redis (atomic via a small Lua script or `MULTI`) is the right default: cheap, one round-trip, and matches the plan-based limits implied by the `plan` column already selected in the auth query. Reach for a sliding-window/token-bucket only if bursty-but-fair traffic matters more than implementation simplicity — that's the one tuning knob worth revisiting later, not now.

Push over polling: use Server-Sent Events (SSE). It's one-way (server to dashboard, which is all this needs), the browser's `EventSource` API auto-reconnects for you, and it rides plain HTTP with no new infra. WebSockets are worth it only if the dashboard needs to send data back (e.g., acknowledging an alert) or you already run one for something else. Polling is the fallback if the backend can't hold long-lived connections (some serverless setups can't).

What's the current stack — backend framework, and how does the dashboard fetch data today? That decides whether this is an SSE endpoint plus an `EventSource` listener, or has to be layered onto existing infra. The other open piece is what triggers a push server-side (DB change stream, pub/sub on writes, or just a periodic broadcast) — that's the next level down once the stack's known.

Recommendation: have the backend push updates over Server-Sent Events (SSE) rather than clients polling — the dashboard opens one long-lived connection and the server emits a message whenever the underlying data changes; the browser just re-renders on each event. Use a plain WebSocket instead only if the dashboard also needs to send data back to the server or updates need to be sub-second.

Two forking decisions: how the client learns data changed, and where "current state" lives.

**Push vs. poll.** For most ops dashboards, short-interval polling (a `fetch` every 5–30s, or a data-fetching library's `refetchInterval`) against the existing REST endpoint is the pragmatic default — no new server infrastructure, works through any proxy/LB, and the staleness window is fine for metrics/status. Reach for SSE or a WebSocket only if data changes faster than your poll interval can track, or if enough dashboards are open concurrently that repeated polling becomes real server load — then the server pushes deltas the moment its own state changes, and you likely also want a message broker (Redis pub/sub, etc.) if there's more than one backend instance.

**Where state lives.** If the dashboard aggregates from multiple sources, decide whether the browser recomputes the view from raw pushed events or a backend service maintains the current aggregate and broadcasts that — the latter keeps the client dumb and avoids drift when a client reconnects mid-stream.

What's the current stack (frontend framework, and does the backend already expose a way to detect "did anything change")? That determines whether polling-with-caching or SSE is less work here.

1. **Idempotency key lifetime** — generate one key per checkout *attempt* (e.g. derived from `order.id`), before the first request, and reuse it across all retries of that attempt. That's what makes a retry safe instead of a second charge; a key generated per-HTTP-call defeats the purpose.
2. **What happens when retries are also exhausted** — since the state is still unknown, `checkout.js` shouldn't ever put `"failed"` in front of the customer for a timeout. The timeout is the real bug: it means the charge outcome is unknown, not failed — retrying blindly against that risks double-charging, so idempotency has to come before backoff.

Design:
- Give each logical charge attempt a stable idempotency key (order ID + attempt number) passed to the processor, so any retry against the same charge is safe even if the first attempt actually succeeded on their end.
- On timeout, don't mark the charge "failed" — mark it "pending/unknown" and reconcile first (query the processor by that key, or wait for its webhook) before deciding to retry.
- Retry only for the retryable class: timeouts, connection errors, 5xx. Declines, insufficient funds, fraud blocks should never retry.
- Run retries as a background job with exponential backoff + jitter and a capped attempt count, not inline in the request — that's what's currently forcing an immediate "payment failed" instead of giving the charge time to resolve.
- Customer sees "processing" during this window, then a final success/failure once reconciled.

The fork points are idempotency-before-retry and sync-vs-async retry; the backoff schedule and attempt cap are just tuning.

The two decisions that fork this:

**1. Don't treat a timeout as a decline.** A timeout means "unknown," not "failed" — the charge may have actually gone through on the processor's side and only the response got lost. Surfacing "payment failed" on a timeout is the bug; it should show "processing" instead.

**2. Move the retry out of the request/response cycle.** On timeout, enqueue a background job keyed by a stable idempotency key (e.g. `order_id:attempt_group`, not a fresh key per retry) rather than retrying synchronously inline. The job first queries the processor for that charge's actual status — if it already succeeded, mark the order paid and stop; only issue a new charge request (same idempotency key) if it genuinely didn't happen. Exponential backoff, capped attempts, then falls into a dead-letter/alert state for manual follow-up. The customer's order flips to paid/failed via webhook or a status poll once the job resolves, not synchronously.

Left out: the specific backoff schedule and max-attempt count, webhook signature verification, and the UI copy/polling mechanism for the "processing" state — those depend on which processor you're on (Stripe's idempotency keys and status semantics differ from, say, a bank gateway).

The core problem: a timeout means you don't know if the charge actually went through on the processor's side, so a naive retry risks double-charging, and showing "payment failed" for what's really "unknown/pending" is misleading the customer.

**Recommendation:** move retries out of the request path into an async job, keyed by idempotency key, with reconciliation before showing failure.

- On charge creation, generate and persist an idempotency key tied to the order/attempt (most processors — Stripe, Braintree, Adyen — support this natively). Every retry reuses the same key, so if the original request actually succeeded downstream, the processor returns the existing result instead of charging twice.
- On timeout, don't tell the customer "failed." Mark the charge `pending_retry` and show something like "processing your payment." Enqueue a background job to retry with backoff (a few attempts over the next 1-2 minutes is usually enough for a transient timeout).
- Before each retry, query the processor for the charge's actual status rather than blind-firing — some timeouts are the processor having succeeded but the response never reaching you, and a status check avoids even a deduped retry call.
- Only transition to `failed` (and tell the customer) after retries are exhausted or the processor returns a genuine decline. Genuine declines shouldn't go through the retry loop at all — retry is for timeouts/network errors, not card-declined.

**The two decisions that actually fork the design:**
1. Reconcile-first (status check before retrying) vs. rely-on-idempotency-key-alone (just retry, let the processor dedupe). Reconcile-first is safer and barely costs more, so default to it unless your processor's idempotency guarantees are airtight.
2. Sync retry (customer's request stays open while you retry) vs. async job (return "processing" immediately, notify on outcome). Given these are already timing out, retrying synchronously just risks a second timeout on the same request — async is the right call here.

Left out: exact backoff schedule/attempt count, and how you notify the customer of the final outcome (webhook/poll/email) — both are tuning, not forks.

The current code treats a timeout as a definite failure (`payments.js:36` → `catch` in `checkout.js:29`), but `PROVIDER.md` says a timeout on `/v2/charges` is not a failure — it's **unknown**, since the vendor may have already authorised the charge before the connection died. Retrying blind risks a double charge; the fix has two decisions:

**1. Idempotency key, scoped to the order and persisted before the first attempt.** Cardstream dedupes on `Idempotency-Key` for 24h and returns the same charge id. Generate the key once per order (e.g. `charge:${order.id}`), write it to the `orders` row *before* calling `charge()`, and send it as the header on every attempt for that order — the in-process retries, and also any later retry (customer re-clicking, a reconciliation job, a server restart after the request already reached the vendor). Without persisting it first, a retry after a process crash has no way to know it's a retry.

**2. What happens when the retry also times out.** Retry the same charge (same key) a bounded number of times with backoff inside the request — but if every attempt times out, don't report "failed": you still don't know the outcome. Report something like "processing" and resolve it out-of-band, either by letting the customer safely hit `/pay` again later (now safe because of the idempotency key) or by a background job that re-sends the same charge with the same key to get the vendor's authoritative answer.

Left out: exact retry count/backoff, whether to add a `payment_attempts` table for audit/observability, and the reconciliation job's schedule.

The timeout risk here isn't "it failed, try again" — PROVIDER.md is explicit that a timed-out charge is **unknown**, not failed, and Cardstream only de-dupes if you send the same `Idempotency-Key` twice. Today `payments.js` sends no key at all, so a naive retry-on-timeout in `checkout.js` would risk authorizing the customer's card twice.

**Recommendation:** persist an idempotency key on the order *before* the first charge attempt (e.g. an `orders.idempotency_key` column, set once), and move the retry loop into `payments.charge()` itself, sending that key on every attempt including retries. Retry only on timeout/network-error/5xx (the "unknown" outcomes per the vendor doc) with a couple of backoff attempts; a 4xx decline is a definite answer and shouldn't retry. `checkout.js`'s existing catch block barely changes — it just now sees fewer timeouts, because most get absorbed by the internal retry instead of surfacing as "payment failed."

2. **What's retryable** — timeout/network/5xx yes, 4xx no, straight from PROVIDER.md's unknown-vs-failed distinction.

Left out: exact retry count/backoff curve, and what the customer sees if all retries still exhaust (still a failure message, but now safe to retry later since the key is stable).

```sql
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vector);
```

```sql
FROM products
WHERE active AND search_vector @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)
ORDER BY ts_rank(search_vector, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)) DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

The core issue: a timeout is not a decline — you don't know whether the charge went through on the processor's side. Retrying blindly risks double-charging, and telling the customer "payment failed" is just wrong when the real state is "unknown."

Design:

1. **Idempotency key per checkout attempt**, sent to the payment processor (e.g., Stripe's `Idempotency-Key`). Any retry against that same attempt is deduped server-side by the processor, so a resend after a timeout can't create a second charge even if your own retry logic fires twice.
2. **Classify the failure before deciding to retry.** Network/timeout errors are retryable-but-ambiguous; hard declines (insufficient funds, fraud block) are not — retrying those is pointless and the customer should see the real reason immediately.
3. **On timeout, don't show "failed."** Show "processing" and reconcile the actual outcome — query the processor for the charge's status using the same idempotency key, or wait for its webhook, before writing a final success/fail state.
4. **Run retries out of the request path** — a background worker with bounded attempts and backoff, not inline in the web request, so the customer connection isn't held open waiting on a slow processor.
5. **Persist attempt state keyed by order/charge id** (pending/retrying/succeeded/failed) so a process restart doesn't lose track, and the webhook or poll result just updates that row.

The one decision that forks the whole shape: reconcile via **webhook** (cheaper, but adds latency and you must handle out-of-order delivery) vs **poll the processor** after each timeout (bounded wait, simpler mental model, more API calls). I'd default to webhook-driven with a short poll fallback if no webhook lands within N seconds.

Left out: tuning the retry count/backoff curve, and how this unifies if you have more than one payment provider.

The immediate bug is showing "payment failed" before retries are exhausted — that's a UX fix, not a retry design. The retry design itself hinges on one thing: a timeout means you don't know if the charge landed on the processor's side, so a naive retry risks double-charging.

**Recommendation:** send every attempt (including retries) with the same idempotency key tied to the original charge intent, so the processor collapses retries into one charge regardless of how many times you resend. Do the retry async — queue the charge, return "processing" to the customer, and update them via webhook/poll — rather than retrying inline in the request, since the whole point is that the processor is slow right now and blocking the customer on more of that latency doesn't help.

The other fork: only retry errors you've classified as transient (timeout, network error, 5xx from the processor). Declines, insufficient funds, and fraud holds are not retryable — retrying those wastes attempts and can trip the processor's fraud detection.

Left out at this level: exponential backoff and a max-attempt cap, and a reconciliation job that checks processor status by idempotency key for charges that timed out on your side but may have actually succeeded upstream (otherwise you can retry into a real double-charge if the idempotency key handling has a gap).

PROVIDER.md is the reason a naive retry is dangerous here: a timeout on `/v2/charges` is explicitly **unknown**, not failed, since the vendor may have authorized before the connection died. Retrying blindly risks a double charge; the fix has to lean on the `Idempotency-Key` header the vendor already supports but we don't send.

1. Generate a stable idempotency key per payment attempt (e.g. `orderId` + attempt), persist it before the first request goes out, and send it on every retry of that attempt. That's what makes retries safe — a retry after a real success returns the original charge instead of authorizing twice.
2. On timeout, don't reject to "failed" — retry the same key with backoff (a few attempts is plenty; you're nowhere near the 600/min limit), and if it still doesn't resolve, persist the order as `payment_unknown`/`processing` rather than `failed`. A real decline (4xx from the provider) is the only case that should surface as "payment failed" to the customer.

What that leaves open: how `payment_unknown` orders get reconciled if all retries in-request also time out (background poll vs. webhook), and where the idempotency key/attempt count live (column on `orders` vs. a separate `payment_attempts` table) — both are schema/ops decisions, not forks in the retry logic itself.

Add a generated `tsvector` column combining `name` (weighted higher) and `description`, with a GIN index:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN search_vec tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', name), 'A') ||
    setweight(to_tsvector('english', description), 'B')
  ) STORED;

CREATE INDEX products_search_vec_idx ON products USING GIN (search_vec);
```

Then a `GET /search?q=` route alongside the existing `GET /` in `routes/products.js`, using `websearch_to_tsquery` (handles multi-word queries the way users actually type them) and ranking:

```sql
SELECT id, sku, name, price_cents
FROM products
WHERE active AND search_vec @@ websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)
ORDER BY ts_rank(search_vec, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $1)) DESC
LIMIT 50 OFFSET $2
```

If the product list is user-facing and typos matter, layer in `pg_trgm` (trigram similarity) either as a fallback when full-text returns nothing, or blended into ranking. Skip it if search is mostly internal/admin.
2. **New endpoint vs extending the existing one.** A separate `/search` route keeps the plain listing query untouched and simple; folding `q` into `GET /` as an optional param avoids a second endpoint but complicates the query branching. Given the existing route is already doing pagination cleanly, I'd keep them separate.

That decision picks between the two options above — everything else (indexing pipeline, ranking tuning) is detail below that line.

2. **Reconcile before retrying**, not after. On timeout, first query the processor for the charge's actual status (or just resend with the same idempotency key and let it return the existing result) before deciding to retry or give up.
3. **Only retry transient errors** — timeouts, 5xx, network errors. Card declines and other definite failures should never retry.

Because the key is the same on every attempt, a retry after a real timeout either completes the original authorization or gets back Cardstream's byte-identical response for the charge that already happened — never a duplicate. `checkout.js` then only needs to call the retrying `charge()` and can drop the "unknown means failed" behavior in the catch block.
